1048481,ca.proc.d.1935-02-07.2.2.4,1935-02-07,e885929f-c4c1-4965-b723-ad4350f8b072,ca.m.5276,Hon. W. A. GORDON (Minister of Labour):,Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines,QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS,PICTOU, N.S. WHARF LUMBER PURCHASED",,"Mr. Speaker, a few days ago the

hon. member for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe) inquired with respect to Canada's permanent seat on the international labour organization, and I promised1 to give the answer as soon as I had the information. With the permission of the house I would like to read a short statement.
Part 13 of the treaty of Versailles, which established the international labour organization, provided that its governing body should

consist of representatives (a) of member states; (b) of employers' organizations, and (c) of workers' organizations. The States represented on the governing body were to be the eight states of chief industrial importance among the members of the international 92582-36
labour organization, who were to have permanent seats on the body, plus a number of states, first four and now eight, elected by the international labour conference for a three year term.

The question of determining which were the eight states of chief industrial importance presented difficulties from the inception of the organization. The first provisional list prepared in 1919 was challenged by a number of governments which thought they should be included in the first eight. It was not then known whether Germany and the United States would become members of the organization, and it was thought inexpedient to proceed to the establishment of a list which, everyone recognized, would require reconsideration if either of these great industrial states joined the international labour organization. Subsequently Germany decided to join the or ganization in 1920, but the United States deferred its application to enter until the summer of 1934.

In 1922 the council of the league to which the question had been referred decided that the eight members of the international labour organization should be Germany, Belgium, Canada, France, Great Britain, India, Italy and Japan. This list was prepared on the basis of seven criteria, namely:

column2: total industrial population (in the strict sense of the term) including the mining and transport industries;
the proportion which the industrial population bears to the whole population;
total horse-power (steam and water power), not including locomotives and vessels;
Horse power per head of population.
Total length of railways;
Length of railways per thousand square kilometres of territory;
Development of the mercantile marine.

column1: The list thus established has been in effect

since 1922. Last year, however, the entry of Russia into the League of Nations, which involved its accession to the international labour organization and the decision of the United States of America to adhere to the international labour organization, created a new situation which was further complicated by the withdrawal of Germany from the league and the international labour organization-subject to two years' notice of denunciation-which will elapse in November, 1935. It was clear to everyone concerned that this new situation would require the preparation of a new list of the eight members of chief industrial importance.
Russian Timber

It was the view of the Canadian government that the determination of the eight states of chief industrial importance was, in the first instance, the function of the international labour conference-a body on which all members of the organization are represented-and which appoints three-quarters of the governing body, and that, consequently, the governing body itself was not warranted in assuming that function. From a careful study of the treaty and of the decisions affecting its interpretation we were led to the conclusion that whatever authority was competent to determine the list of eight states, this list should only be revised when the three-year term of the elected members of the governing body had expired. Finally, the question arose as to the criteria to be adopted.

These problems, primarily of a legal and constitutional nature arising out of the interpretation of the relevant parts of the treaty of Versailles and of the opinions expressed on earlier occasions in the council of the League of Nations, have been the subject of careful consideration by the government. They were discussed with representatives of the international labour organization in Geneva by the Canadian delegation to the last assembly of the league. We have since kept in close touch with the discussions which preceded the last meeting of the governing body, at which it was decided to revise the list of eight states of chief industrial importance, and bring the revised list into force at the first opportunity. Our concern in these discussions has been to see that the international labour organization remained constant to its constitution as it was laid down by the labour articles of the treaty and has been interpreted by the competent authorities established for that purpose.

The legal and constitutional questions raised in the course of the consideration of this question are of importance to the smooth functioning of the international labour organization. and the government are considering the advisability of requesting that steps be taken to clarify and place on a definite and unmistakable basis the procedure to be followed in determining at what periods and in what manner the list of eight states should be revised in future.

At the session of the governing body which ended on January 31, the governing body adopted a revised list of eight countries of chief industrial importance, namely the United States, Great Britain, Germany, France, India, Russia, Italy and Japan, and voted unanimously to accord Canada and Belgium

seats on the governing body as deputy members until 1937. This solution of a difficult question has the great merit of securing the close cooperation and responsibility of the United States in the work of an organization with which Canada has been associated from the beginning and to which it is the policy of this government to give unwavering support. Nevertheless the constitutional administrative question cannot be said to be satisfactorily settled.

The correspondence that passed between the government and our representative at Geneva I regret to say I will not table because in the past it has never been the practice to table communications of that character, as they have been held to be confidential communications between a government and its representative.

1048484,ca.proc.d.1935-02-07.3.2,1935-02-07,b9296f13-96f7-4c62-a577-63a5fc91ac2f,ca.m.6164,Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister):,Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs,BRITISH IMPORTS OF RUSSIAN TIMBER,,,Mr. Speaker, last evening the junior member for Ottawa (Mr. Ahearn) directed the attention of the house to a report in a newspaper respecting trade arrangements made between Timber Distributors Limited of Great Britain and the Soviet Union. I observe he placed upon the record a clipping from the newspaper which reads:
Deal concluded between Great Britain and Soviet. Canada to lose lumber trade. Fifty per cent of Canadian export to Britain in 1935 threatened.

It is difficult to understand just why any newspaper should make any statement of the kind which is not borne out by the article in question. No deal or contract has been made between Great Britain and the Soviet Union. Timber Distributors Limited is a joint stock company operated, as I understand it, in Great Britain. Its members are largely dealers in timber. They have for a period of years made contracts for the delivery of supplies of timber from Russia to their yards in Great Britain which they, in turn, have sold to customers. There has been inserted in such contracts a provision known as the ""fall clause,"" and under the provisions of an article in the Ottawa agreements the Canadian government is given the right to protest to the British government if as a result of the introduction of that clause into the contract the preference which is granted to Canada under the Ottawa agreement made with Great Britain is prejudicially or injuriously affected.
Last year we did protest against the so-called ""fall clause"" and other terms of the
Empire Trade Agreements

contract made between the private enterprise known as Timber Distributors Limited and the Russian Soviet. As a result the board of trade determined on a middle course, and the obnoxious clause was eliminated, with the result that we secured a market for a very large quantity of timber in Great Britain. Of course we have nothing to do with the contracts which may be entered into between a private enterprise and the Soviet Union. They may make any contract they wish. But having made the contract, if it prejudicially affects the interests of Canadian shippers we then call upon the British government to take such steps as may be necessary to remedy the injury which may be done. Great Britain has secured for the executive from parliament the power to enable them to deal with the situation when necessity arises. We have already filed with the board of trade a statement indicating what the position of Canada is with respect to any contract which contains the fall clause or prejudicially affects the interests of our country in connection with the export of timber.

1048491,ca.proc.d.1935-02-07.5.1.2,1935-02-07,b1d5c682-1934-44e3-8c98-235be860bb63,ca.m.3501,Mr. J. L. BROWN (Lisgar):,,EMPIRE TRADE AGREEMENTS,"PROPOSED APPROVAL OF OPERATION OF AGREEMENTS CONCLUDED AT IMPERIAL ECONOMIC CONFERENCE, 1932",,"Mr. Speaker, the resolution presently before the house calling upon us to endorse the Ottawa trade agreements of 1932 was, I have no doubt, put upon the order paper at the instigation of the government. Certainly it was put there with the government's hearty approval.

The purpose in putting this resolution on the order paper is abundantly clear. It was no doubt expected that it would greatly embarrass the members of the opposition to vote against the motion, but for my part, Mr. Speaker, I have not the slightest hesitation in accepting the challenge.

The objections that were urged against the Ottawa trade agreements in 1932 still hold. The right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) has made it abundantly clear that those fundamental principles underlying these agreements to which we objected in 1932 are still there, and still open to all the objections that we urged at that time. In my judgment a great opportunity was missed at that Ottawa conference. It is not given to every man to have the opportunity to correct his blunders, but there was given to the Prime Minister the opportunity to correct the great blunder that he made at the first conference to which he went in England in 1930. But instead of embracing that opportunity he continued still to blunder, and the result was that the Ottawa agreements were built upon an utterly unsound foundation.

I had the pleasure of listening to the speech that was made by the Right Hon. Stanley Baldwin at the opening of the conference. I was sitting in a garage in a little town out in Manitoba at the time, and when I heard Mr. Baldwin's speech it filled me with delight. Stanley Baldwin expressed the hope that the agreements would be based upon reductions of tariffs rather than upon increases, but unfortunately the attitude of the Prime Minister of Canada was entirely different. He insisted that the agreements should be based upon an entirely different principle, and it is an open secret that on more than one occasion the Ottawa conference was on the verge of collapse. I have not the slightest doubt that had it not been for the spectacle which Great Britain and the dominions would have presented to the world if the imperial statesmen had gone home without an agreement, that actually that would have been the result, but it was simply impossible that the conference should disband without some agreement at least being arrived at; and so, Mr. Speaker, instead of calling those agreements, as the Minister of Trade and Com-
Empire Trade Agreements

merce (Mr. Hanson) did, the bulwark of our trade, I say that they are a house built upon the sand rather than upon the solid rock of good will. There is no issue that I would welcome more heartily, no issue on which I would more gladly conduct a campaign in my constituency than the Ottawa agreements and the difference in the attitude of the two political parties on the question of an imperial preference.

I wish to discuss these agreements from two aspects; first, their effect on the revenue and the burden of taxation; and secondly, the supposed effect of the six cents preference on wheat. But first I should like to make a few general remarks.

It is a false assumption that everything that has happened since the Ottawa agreements has been the result of those agreements. It is a very common thing for people who do not reason closely to say that, because such and such a thing was done, therefore this is the result. I know that the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) is well aware that the most common fallacy that is known in logic is ""post hoc, ergo propter hoc."" It is the most common fallacy to assume that because such and such a thing happened or was done that everything that subsequently followed was the result of that preceding event. It has been pointed out by the right hon. leader of the opposition that we have that fallacy to-day, the assumption that because certain things have happened in connection with our trade they are necessarily the result of the Ottawa agreements. But, Mr. Speaker, there are many other factors that have entered into the problem and these must be taken into account. Every factor must be given due consideration in endeavouring to come to a conclusion on questions such as these.

I might also point out that very often we have an entirely wrong use made of statistics. It is one thing to quote at length statistics that may be right or wrong-we will admit that they are right-but it is another thing *entirely to draw correct conclusions from those statistics. It is one thing to recognize facts, and an entirely different thing to draw the proper conclusion from those facts. We have had statistics presented to the house but we found that the conclusions drawn from them were entirely wrong. First I should like to refer to the speech of the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) who spent almost an hour

and a half trying to convince the house-and I imagine this side of the house in particular -that while for several weeks he opposed this legislation and voted against it, together with his party, he really favours the agreement. Yet, while he now states more clearly than ever that he is in favour of these agreements, apparently he is going to vote against the resolution. I must say that the right hon. gentleman did not convince me that this was the right attitude to take, and even if he had done so it simply would have meant that he has not the full support of the hon. members who sit behind him.

In my opinion there is one hon. member who deserves congratulations; I refer to the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid). The hon. member certainly put a great many words in his speech, which indicates that he is a great worker, and I should like to congratulate him on the labour he devoted to his address. I am not going to traverse the ground the hon. gentleman covered, except to say that many of his comparisons were not fair. For example, many of his comparisons were made in dollars. The hon. gentleman knows very well, as every hon. member knows, that because of the general decrease in commodity prices throughout the world comparisons in dollars are not fair and do not give a true picture of the situation. Others of his comparisons were between different years, which always leads to wrong conclusions. In my opinion the only

He referred first to butter and other dairy products and then to cattle.

First of all I should like to correct an observation I heard him make, and which appears in Hansard to the effect that under the King administration the duty on butter was four cents a pound. The remark may have been unintentional, and if he were present I should be quite whiling to accept his denial. The hon. member knew very well however that under the King administration the duty on foreign butter was only one cent per pound, and if he was mistaken I think he should have made a correction in Hansard.

I protest further against the affirmation made not only by the hon. member for Sherbrooke but by many hon. members to your left, Mr. Speaker, that the Prime Minister and the Conservative party generally, during the campaign of 1930 promised the Canadian farmers that if that party were returned to power the farmers would receive from 50 to 60 cents per pound for their butter.

I absolutely deny that statement, and I deny it every time I have a chance. I never made it, and throughout the whole election campaign I never heard the Prime Minister make it. I believe I may state safely that he never made it at any time. What I heard him say and what I said was that if the Conservative party were returned to office in 1930 the government would see to it that the Canadian farmer and the Canadian dairyman obtained the Canadian market for themselves.

Then the hon. member for Sherbrooke went on to say that we promised we would stop importations of butter, and indicated that during 1934 we imported about 2,000,000 pounds. I have not his exact figures before me, but I believe I am about correct. But he did not say why we imported it. I wish hon. members would tell us why, because I am prepared to tell them. Why did we import any quantity-for the sake of argument we will say 2,000,000 pounds -in 1934, if in fact we did import it? Will any hon. member opposite deny that on every pound of butter imported during 1934 there was a duty of five cents per pound and a special tax of three cents, making a total of eight cents per pound? They will not deny it, because it is a fact which cannot be denied. How is it that New Zealand or any other country exported butter to Canada? We know that the people of New Zealand had a free market in England for their butter, and if so why did they export to this country? Why? There was only one reason, and that is that the Canadian market price for butter was so much higher than the price in Great Britain that New Zealand could export to this country, pay the duty and bring more money to their farmers than they could by shipping to England.

If instead of taxing eight cents per pound we had taxed only one cent would the Canadian farmer be in any better position to-day? Where would the Canadian farmer be to-day if there had not been a duty of eight cents a pound on butter? There would have been only one result: Our price would have been reduced by eight cents; the Canadian price of 23 cents per pound would have been only 15 cents, had there been no protection. 1048548,ca.proc.d.1935-02-07.5.1.59,1935-02-07,2d8bf138-dba3-41dc-9222-42ece3116f57,ca.m.8339,Mr. GOBEIL:,,EMPIRE TRADE AGREEMENTS,PROPOSED APPROVAL OF OPERATION OF AGREEMENTS CONCLUDED AT IMPERIAL ECONOMIC CONFERENCE, 1932",,"He had the audacity to ask the government, ""What did you do when you found that the American market was closed to us?"" Why did he not finish his observation by saying that without a word of protest the Liberal government allowed the Canadian farmer to be excluded from the American market, because that government would not act for fear of provoking the Yankees. Does the hon. member for Sherbrooke realize what the Canadian farmer lost when the American market was closed to him? Does he really know what it meant? I do not think he does, because if he had such information he would not dare mention the subject. In the twelve months previous to June, 1930, the fresh milk and cream made into butter and exported amounted to 25,000,000 pounds. That is what we lost. That market was not lost through any fault of this government but through the fault of the previous administration. If someone is to be blamed it must be hon. members opposite. Owing to that market being closed, in the twelve following months the Canadian market had to absorb
25,000,000 pounds of butter which previously had been shipped to the United States. That is what we lost when we lost the American market.

The hon. member for Sherbrooke also mentioned cattle. Again I ask him, does he realize what it meant to the Canadian farmer to lose that market, and again I say, under the King administration. It meant that while in the twelve months previous to June, 1930, we exported to the United States almost 300,000 head of cattle, in the following year we exported less than 10,000 head. Was that the fault of this government? No, nobody will pretend that it was the fault of this government. Is it any wonder that the situation of the producers of beef and cattle in Canada was almost desperate when we lost such a valuable market without a protest- or at least without any protest that the citizens of this country know of? Those are only two items, Mr. Speaker. I could go on and mention almost every farm product against which we found the doors absolutely closed to us in June of 1930, and for that hon. members opposite are now trying to hold this government responsible, but they are mistaken. Is it possible that hon. members opposite so misjudge the good common sense of Canadians as to think that the people will believe them when they say that this government has closed the avenues of trade? Do they believe that the Canadian people will believe that without specific instances being given without mentioning at least some countries that have raised their tariffs against us since 1930? No, Mr. Speaker, hon. gentlemen opposite are greatly mistaken if they think they are going to be taken at their word.

What else did it mean when the American market was closed to us? What other signification did it have? What were the results in the following months? What was the balance of trade between Canada and the United States in the fiscal year 1930-31? We lost the American market only in June. The result was this, that in that fiscal year we had an adverse balance of trade with the United States of over S300.000.000. Do hon. mentbers opposite believe that such a situation could go on indefinitely? When the hon. member for Sherbrooke asks this government ""What did you do?"" I reply that this Conservative 'government took means to correct that adverse balance of trade against Canada. It had to be corrected, and as a result of the efforts of this government instead of having an adverse of balance of trade of over $300,000.000, that had been reduced in 1932 to $87,836,456, and in 1934, last year, it had been reduced further to S49,127,522, and that was done because of the imperial agreements
Empire Trade Agreements
which give us a sheltered market in the United Kingdom for the products of the farm that we could no longer ship to the United States.

My hon. friends opposite have another argument, and it is this. They say that these agreements prevent trade with other countries, and I have heard them say that they make impossible a trade treaty with the United States, for instance. I shall not have time to make any extended remarks upon that, but let me just quote from an American newspaper to show what the people over there think of the possibilities of trade with Canada, despite the Ottawa agreements. I quote from the Boston Sunday Advertiser:

The Ottawa empire agreements, contrary to general belief, leave ample room for Canadian-American trade. There is nothing in them to prevent Canada selling the United States more of her cattle, more of her fish, more of her milk and of copper and lumber,

and so on and so forth. That is the opinion of the Americans, but that paper goes further and, referring to the Ottawa agreements, says that, not only have they been beneficial to Canada but that they have brought to Canada more industries and given Canadians more employment. In other words, if it had not been for those agreements unemployment would have been much more severe than it is. This newspaper goes on to say:
In 1932 American branch factories established themselves in the dominion at the rate of two each week.

They crossed the border, Mr. Speaker, to sscape the Canadian tariff or to secure the benefit of the empire preference, and the loss to the United States in work and wages must have been enormous. This paper goes further and says:

To-day there are something like 1,500 of these United States branch plants in Canada, representing an investment of nearly two billion dollars and giving employment to scores of thousands of Canadians.
That is not my statement, Mr. Speaker, nor that of a member of this government, but the opinion of our neighbour to the south.

I can quite understand that the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) did not see with any very great pleasure this resolution on the order paper. We can all understand that. As I said at the beginning of my remarks, even if the right hon. gentleman had succeeded in convincing me, despite his opposition to the legislation and his vote against it two years ago, that he was in favour of these agreements to-day, that would only demonstrate one thing and that is the lack of unity among

his followers. I shall try to give one or two-illustrations. Every member of this house must have noticed the change of tone in the speeches of the right hon. leader of the opposition with respect to these agreements. It is quite clear to anyone that he is now more in favour of these agreements than he was in. 1932. Is it a spontaneous conversion, or is there something behind it? I have it in my mind that it might be something else than: spontaneous conversion because I remember that in June of 1933 a Liberal organization with a pompous name, I believe it is called the Twentieth Century Young Liberals Association of Canada, or something of the kind, met in Ottawa for two or three days and' passed some resolutions among which was one which did not seem to be quite in accord with the opinion expressed by the leader of the Liberal party in 1932. I would refer hon. members to the Montreal Gazette of June 3, 1933. The convention turned down the resolution submitted to it, that the Liberal' party should do its utmost to abrogate the treaties entered into at the Ottawa conference. That Liberal convention, in my view, passed a resolution disapproving of the opinion that was expressed in this house by their leader in 1932.

Now, speaking of unity of sentiment and of the endorsation or the disapproval of the Ottawa agreements by the Liberal party I am going to remind the house of some of the statements that were made by hon. gentlemen opposite. First, I will quote from page 355 of Hansard of 1932 to show what the hon. member for Melville (Mr. Motherwell) said in reference to hogs, when he was discussing these agreements:
But they started out in the face of hogs selling at about 2} cents a pound-
What does he think of the price of hogs to-day?
-trying to start a campaign to bring about greater production, based on something by way of restriction that may never materialize.
Apparently it has materialized.

It is stated by the Prime Minister that in ten years we will have a potential market for 590,000 hogs, but those same potentialities extend to other countries. We would need to eat little but bacon and ham if we were to consume the products of a campaign such as this.
Then he went on to say this:
It is the greatest piece of nonsense that was ever promulgated,-
What does he think of it now?
-the greatest flimflam ever attempted to be put over on a suffering people. There is no
Empire Trade Agreements
more comfort in it than there is in a block of ice in midwinter.
I am afraid the block of ice has melted. Further on, at page 356, he said:

I did not think there was an aggregation of men in the world, either inside or outside a mental hospital, who would promulgate such a nonsensical proposition as this hog proposal as set out in the agreement.

What does he think of it now that hogs are selling at 8^ or 9 cents a pound, representing an additional 87,000,000 going into the pockets of Canadian farmers, who are receiving altogether around $30,000,000 or $35,000,000 of added money since 1932? I will quote another hon. member opposite. At page 605 of Hansard of the same year the hon. member for South Perth (Mr. Sanderson) made this statement:
Is there a single commitment in that article, Mr. Speaker-
He was referring to hogs.

-which obliges his majesty's government in the United Kingdom to increase the purchase of *Canadian bacon and ham? This provision is surrounded by ifs and whens and hows, and in any event nothing can be done until the report of this commission is brought in. I want to make this prediction,-
Let me remind him now of the prediction he made then, and ask him what he thinks *of it.

-that if in course of time the export of Canadian bacon and ham should reach the figure mentioned in article 6, the farmers all over this dominion will go into hog raising on a large scale, and instead of increasing the price of hogs the price will decrease. The price is $3.75 now, and it may go even lower.

That was the price in 1932 when we were *discussing the agreements. Apparently we have not yet reached the stage referred to by the hon. gentleman, when the raising of more hogs results in a decrease in price.

Now, so far as unity of thinking is concerned, I wish to quote some words uttered by the leader of the opposition-always with reference to the imperial agreements. The house will remember that the leader of the opposition spent at least an hour telling us how dreadful it was for the present Prime Minister to have terrorized Englishmen to the extent that he had done, until they had to yield to his whip. It seems to me that was rather a compliment, though the right hon* gentleman was far from thinking that way. Let me quote some of the phrases he used as reported at page 266 of Hansard of that year:
If we have reached the point in our history where the thought of public men not only in this country but in all parts of the empire is to be terrorized by the Prime Minister of

Canada, it is time that some of us should speak out and let the people of Great Britain know that the people of Canada are just as proud of an independent expression of view as are the people of Great Britain.
And on page 267, referring to the Prime Minister, the right hon. gentleman said:
He said to Great Britain, ""You must change your fiscal policy before I will negotiate with you."" He now says to us, ""You must change your principles or you cannot support this agreement,""
Apparently they have changed their principles, because they support the agreement now. He went on:
The fiscal policy of Great Britain has been changed. Whether the right hon. gentleman was responsible for changing it is a matter of indifference; the fact remains that it has been changed.

The leader of the opposition was very much exercised over the fact that, according to him, the Prime Minister had imposed his will on Englishmen and terrorized and coerced them. That may be all very well in this house, but not in the country. The board of strategy, or the leader of the Liberal members from Quebec-sometimes they refer to the hon. member for Quebec East as their leader- evidently decided that these phrases were not very popular in that province, that they would not get them anywhere, and apparently therefore they deputed someone to make a different declaration, with the result that we find the following statement coming from the hon. member for St. James (Mr. Rinfret), ex-Secretary of State, as reported at page 376 of Hansard:

In my opinion articles 12, 13, and 14 dealing with the tariff board are most extraordinary. I say this is the first time any other country, even if it be the United Kingdom, has been given the right by means of a commercial treaty to dictate to the government of this country concerning certain Canadian matters.
How do my hon. friends reconcile these different expressions of opinion? The hon. gentleman went further and made this statement :
Under the provisions of these articles we are being dictated to-
The leader of the opposition declared that the Prime Minister had terrorized the English at the imperial conference, but the hon. member for St. James says:

-we are being dictated to by an external government and it makes no difference whether this dictation comes from the government of the United Kingdom, of France or any other country. We are being dictated to ... I may be all wrong about this, Mr. Speaker, but I think it is abominable that the government
Empire Trade Agreements
of Canada should be told in a trade agreement by another nation, that they shall do certain things of a local character.
What does my hon. friend think of these two statements?
^ The next move I suppose on the part of Great Britain will be to have what gentlemen they want on that board. That would not be any worse.
And further on:

Have I read that aright, Mr. Speaker? If so, not only are we being dictated to by another government to appoint a board entirely local in its character, but here are the instructions by which the board is to be bound.

And he goes on. I am stating this not particularly that the house may know because we have already heard it, but that the citizens of Canada may know the policy of the Liberal party, their disagreement among themselves on Canadian policies or the policies of their leader.

GOLDING (South Huron):,,EMPIRE TRADE AGREEMENTS,PROPOSED APPROVAL OF OPERATION OF AGREEMENTS CONCLUDED AT IMPERIAL ECONOMIC CONFERENCE, 1932",,"Mr. Speaker, as a result of the resolution which stands on the order paper in the name of the hon. member for Toronto-Scarborough (Mr. Harris), we are having a further discussion on the empire treaties. It opens up another discussion on some of the principles for which members of the house stand and it is in regard to those principles that a difference of opinion exists in connection with these particular treaties. I think it is generally agreed that we are all in favour of empire trade, but it is on the basis upon which this trade is formed, the regulations surrounding it and its effect on world trade that there is a distinct difference of opinion. I do not think for a moment our hon. friends opposite will suggest that we on this side are not in favour of empire trade, nor do I believe they will suggest that had the Liberal party been returned to power in 1930, we would not have had empire trade agreements effected; I do not think that is the contention. I would like to point out that in 1930 the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) certainly did succeed in making the Canadian people believe he had definite plans and policies which, if put into effect in this country, would solve all our problems, that markets would be secured for our basic products and prices for those products would be increased. Notwithstanding what the hon. member for Compton (Mr. Gobeil) has said, the fact of the matter is that the Prime Minister went up and down this country telling the people that prices of all farm commodities and other products

would be increased. I would like my hon. friend to visit the village of Exeter in my constituency and ask the people there what the Prime Minister had to say about increased prices. Other promises of the right hon. gentleman may be cited. For instance unemployment was going to be ended, and as a matter of fact all our problems were going to vanish like the melting snows on a sunny morn. I think it was generally believed he based his hopes on changing the tariff structure of this country in order to bring about these improvements. It is a fact that the present treaties are founded on the principles upon which the Conservative party hoped to fulfil the many promises given to the electors at that time.

The extent to which the increased barriers to trade were brought into effect as a result of these treaties, restricting our opportunities of promoting trade with other countries, I think is a fair question for debate. We on this side of the house believe mutual trade, and also our prospects of promoting trade elsewhere, were thereby affected. That too is a fair subject for debate. Holding that view, we opposed the treaties in 1932 and we are still of the same opinion. We feel that these treaties under their present set-up with the existing regulations will affect trade and therefore we believe they are not operating in the best interests of Canada. The hon. member for Compton suggested that we should name some countries that have raised their tariffs since these treaties have come into effect. The hon. member for Yorkton (Mr. McPhee) in one of his speeches put on the records of the house the fact that thirty-seven countries had raised their duties against Canada.

We recall the promises that were made in 1930 and now we are told that conditions are improving. We were told the same thing in 1931, 1932, 1933 and 1934. I am willing to admit there is some improvement in trade, but a similar condition exists in every other country and we are glad it does. Notwithstanding that all these promises were made in regard in promoting trade and solving our problems, what is the situation confronting us to-day? I suppose if there is any improvement, it will be credited to the empire trade agreements. It is rather amusing to listen to some of the statements, some of the addresses that have been made in connection with these treaties and some of the propaganda that has been circulated. One would think this government two years ago discovered a brand new market, one that did not exist before.
Empire Trade Agreements

As a matter of fact that market was free to Canada long before many of us saw the light of day and in all probability it will continue to be, I will not say a free market, but a market, whether these treaties are modified or amended or in the years to come discarded altogether. But what is our situation at the present time? It is simply this, that there is not one problem that was facing this country in 1930 that is not still our problem. One can go right down the list and I think my hon. friends will agree with me when I say that all the problems that were facing us at that time are still confronting us. Take the problem of our trade. Does anyone in the house suggest that the problem of finding markets for our exports has been solved? Take the problem of our taxation, and debt. Does anyone suggest that it is solved? We all know it is more serious now than when this government came into power. Take our unemployment problem, that is one that was going to be definitely ended; but a few days ago the Prime Minister admitted that there are now 400,000 unemployed, while the hon. member for North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps) says there are at least 600,000, and the Prime Minister admits that when they came into office the number was 117,000.

Then we have the railway problem. Is that solved? What about the problems with which our farmers and wage earners are faced? It seems to me that the difficulties of our farmers during the lifetime of this government have been more serious than at any other time in our history The very fact that for a whole day here recently member after member arose to ask help for the farmers in their distress is surely evidence enough that that problem has not been solved. The fact that the government find it necessary to bring down a bill to provide 890,000,000 to assist the farmers shows how far this problem is from solution by the government and the Prime Minister who definitely promised to end unemployment and cure all the ills of the farmers. That is the situation, I venture to say no one will dispute it. I fully appreciate the fact that all of us have hopes and ambitions to accomplish certain things, and may have definite plans and ideas for doing it, but difficulties may arise which shatter those hopes and plans. That is the position in which the present government find themselves. Probably they did have some plan or idea by which they hoped to solve our problems. But after four and a half years of fair trial, facts and figures showing that they have absolutely failed, I cannot for the life of me understand how they expect hon. members of this house or the people of the country to believe that further

experimentation with or application of those plans is going to do what they have failed to accomplish during the last four and a half years, or in fact at any time they have been tried since confederation. It seems to me the government would strengthen their position if they frankly admitted that the plans with which they hoped to cure the ills of this country have failed, and would now adopt some other method.

In regard to this present resolution, and the address given by the Prime Minister in Brock-ville early in December-I link the two together because I think that address was just a forerunner of this resolution-I have something to say. I read the report of the Prime Minister's speech with considerable interest. He intimated that one of the major issues in the coming campaign would be the empire trade agreements. Perhaps I should not put it just that way, but should say that the attitude of the opposition towards those treaties was going to be a major issue. Well, I am like the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Brown)
I welcome any discussion of these treaties in my constituency.

I think it ought to be clearly understood that as far as we on this side are concerned we oppose these treaties, on various grounds. But one of the grounds was that the duties against British goods were far too high, and those against foreign goods were absolutely ridiculous.

There is another thing I should like to mention. I think it would be quite impossible for anyone to read the Prime Minister's introduction of these treaties in this house without noticing the provocative and boastful language he used on that occasion. One cannot help but question the sincerity of anyone making such a request.

I think at that time every member of the official opposition had in mind the action of the government in raising duties to such heights in 1930 and 1931, and again under these treaties, as well as pegging the duties on a great many articles for a period of five years, together with all the other frills such as specific duties, excise duties, dumping duties, arbitrary valuation for duty purposes and all the other things that have helped create the difficulties and restrictions in connection with trade. I think there is another thing we should remember, and it is that the Liberal party introduced this preferential policy in the first place while the Conservatives at that time opposed it. We ought to remember also that the Dunning budget, which was so favourably received by the British press, was introduced by the Liberal party. I am not going to discuss the contents of that budget except to say that the gist of it knocks galley west, if I may use that term, the argument that we on this side of the house are not in favour of empire trade, and by the way that argument is being used on our back concessions. I think every Canadian citizen hoped that as a result of the 1932 imperial economic conference trade barriers would be lowered. It was not only Canadians who expressed that hope; I should like to quote the words of Right Hon. Stanley Baldwin, who said:

There are two ways in which increased preference can be given-either by lowering barriers among themselves or by raising them against others. The choice between these two must be governed largely by local considerations, but subject to that, it seems to us that we should endeavour to follow the first rather than the second course. For however great our resources, we cannot isolate ourselves from the world. No nation or group of nations, however wealthy and populous, can maintain prosperity in a world where depression and impoverishment reign. Let us therefore aim at the lowering rather than the raising of barriers, even if we cannot fully achieve our purpose now, and let us remember that any action we take here is bound to have its reactions elsewhere.

That was the position taken by Right Hon. 'Stanley Baldwin, but it was not the position taken by our representatives, and as a result of their action and of these treaties there is no question that trade has been restricted and
our opportunities for promoting trade lessened. 1 think we should1 ask ourselves this question, which I think is fair and reasonable:
column2: Supposing our delegation had

column1: accepted the suggestion of Mr. Baldwin and the conference had agreed to lower trade barriers. Would it not have had the effect of stimulating trade not only within the empire but with the whole world? Further than that, when the whole world was trying to raise tariffs, if the empire had set the example and lowered tariffs would it not have had the effect of opening up channels of trade in many other countries? Let us look at the other picture. The very fact that the British empire agreed to raise trade barriers had its effect on trade both inside end outside the empire; it had the effect of making every country cover up, and the vicious circle continued. It seems to me that we could have done a great deal more effective blasting, if that is the term you want to use, by lowering trade barriers at that time than we have been able to do by raising them. Further than that I cannot see how we can expect to gain access to markets by shutting out goods from those same markets, by publicly admitting that certain actions were taken to shut out the foreigner, and by openly stating that every nation wanting to do business with the British empire must pay tribute for that privilege. If does seem to me that these are damaging statements,

and that it will take a good deal of scientific blasting to overcome their effects.
Now I should like to refer to some statements made by the Prime Minister when he introduced these treaties. He said:

I have not yet touched on that farm commodity which is at the moment of most immediate importance to this country. Finding wheat and flour markets is the great problem facing our wheat growers to-day.

Then he went on to tell us that we had secured free entry for wheat as against a duty of six cents a bushel against foreign countries, and that on flour we had secured free entry as against a ten per cent duty against foreigners. Then he added:
Our secured place in the British flour market means that British domestic millers can only compete with the Canadian flour if they use Canadian wheat standards.

ROBERT WEIR (Minister of Agriculture) :,Minister of Agriculture,EMPIRE TRADE AGREEMENTS,PROPOSED APPROVAL OF OPERATION OF AGREEMENTS CONCLUDED AT IMPERIAL ECONOMIC CONFERENCE, 1932",,"Mr. Speaker, in rising to make a very few observations I take this opportunity to congratulate the hon. member for Toronto-Scarborough (Mr. Harris) for having moved this resolution. I really believe that in so doing he was prompted by the thought that is in the minds of the majority of the people of the Dominion of Canada, and that is a desire to know definitely where the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) and his party in this house stand with reference to the Ottawa agreements.

I listened to the speech of the right hon. leader of the opposition the other night. I thought it was an able speech, considering the subject, and I have read it and reread it since; but I cannot for the life of me tell definitely what his attitude is towards these agreements or what he would do in regard to them if he were prime minister of this country.

I should also like to compliment the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid) for his industry in going through a long list of exports and imports to select a few specified ones such as rice and the odd carload of barley to show that there was not an increase in our export trade in all commodities. It is not necessary for me to deal with what the hon. member for New Westminster said, because his argument could not have been more completely annihilated than it was by his right hon. leader in the first few minutes of his speech, in which he said, not simply that trade had increased since the Ottawa agreements, but that in the last year alone, from October 31, 1933, to October 31, 1934, our trade with the United Kingdom had increased in the neighbourhood of $90,000,000.

I should also like to congratulate the hon. member for Sherbrooke (Mr. Howard)-and I am sorry he is not in his seat to-day, not because I wish him particularly to be present for my congratulations but rather that in his absence I do not feel like making some remarks I would otherwise have made-I should like to congratulate him on making one of the best efforts that could be made in denunciation of the policy of his right hon. leader during the period of nine years when he was Prime Minister of this country, particularly as regards a market for our live stock and dairy products.

The right hon. leader of the opposition stated at the commencement of his address that he felt it would be fairer for purposes of comparison, rather than to take the low point of the depression, 1932, and compare it with the present, to make the comparison between the time he and his government went out of power and the present time. To show you how fair the right hon. gentleman was in those remarks, and also that we may have a clear picture of the situation that confronted this government with reference to markets for our agricultural products, I should like to put on record as shortly as possible what did happen as far as the restrictions of our trade is concerned during the period of nine years when the present leader of the opposition was head of the government in this country; and I shall deal in this connection only with agricultural products. I want to show the restrictions and barriers that had been set up against our trade in agricultural products during the nine years, from 1921 to 1930, that the Liberals were in office-and they were barriers just as insuperable as though stone walls had been built without gates in them between the United States and this country. May I add that I fail to find record of any protest, however slight, on the part of hon. gentlemen opposite against the action of our neighbour to the south in thus shutting their markets to us, or any effort on the part of the Liberal government to have those barriers removed. Take the number of inspected slaughterings of live stock from 1931 to 1934-not estimates, but actual slaughterings in the inspected packing plants. There was an increase in 1934 of over

And it was because of the increase in the price of hogs and the decrease in the price of beef, in comparison, which had caused less bacon and more beef to be consumed, that there has resulted in the past three years an increase in the price, at the end of each year, not only of bacon but also of cattle. For the week ended December 22, 1932, the price of choice steers in Toronto was from $3.90 to $4.50 per hundred; for the week ended December 22, 1933, it was $4.50 to $5.50; and for the week ended December 22, 1934, it was $5 to $5.65, the reason for the increase being as I have stated.

What has been the effect in dollars and cents of this increase in our hog prices in the dominion, admitting that the only factor that has increased the price of hogs has been that preferential market which we have received? 1048583,ca.proc.d.1935-02-07.9.9,1935-02-07,667b40b9-ef5d-47c3-a20c-f7861f720a4f,ca.m.5238,Mr. WEIR (Melfort):,Minister of Agriculture,CANADA'S EXPORTS TO NEW ZEALAND,,,Mr. Speaker, when the house took recess at six o'clock I had dealt with one of the major arguments presented by the right hon. leader of the opposition. Nothing could be better evidence of how difficult it was for the right hon. gentleman to find arguments than the fact that he was forced to select the arguments he did, because they vindicate the stand taken by the manufacturers before 1930 that if they were assured of some tariff stability they could produce goods more cheaply and secure wider markets.

The next argument presented by the right hon. gentleman is an even better demonstration of how difficult he found it to discover anything to say against the Ottawa agreements. He had to travel all the way to the state of western Australia in an endeavour to find an argument against these agreements. He suggested that western Australia asked for separation from Australia oecause of these agreements. The referendum on the subject of separation was granted to the people of that state by a Conservative government and the vote was held in 1932, so the Ottawa agreements had nothing whatever to do with it. Although the referendum was carried the government that granted the referendum was defeated while the party that took a stand against the referendum was returned to power.

The right hon. gentleman next criticized this government for taking to itself the rights of parliament. This I deny absolutely. This government never has taken any step without having received the sanction of parliament,
but what was the record of my right hon. friend when his government was in power? I hold in my hand a copy of an order in council dated at Government House, Ottawa, September 26, 1925, which reads:
Present
The Deputy of His Excellency The Governor General in Council

The Deputy of His Excellency the Governor General in Council, on the recommendation of the Minister of Finance, is pleased to order that under the provisions of section 5 of The Australian Trade Agreement Act, 1925, and sulbject to the provisions of the said act, the rates of duties set out in schedule 2 to the said act shall be and the same are hereby extended to goods the produce or manufacture of New Zealand when imported into Canada.
Without even bringing the matter before parliament the government of the right hon. gentleman changed treaties to such an extent as to make a complete new treaty.

Then the right hon. gentleman dealt at some length with the attitude of the Prime Minister during the conference. In reading from the statement by Right Hon. Stanley Baldwin my right hon. friend was careful to read only that part that suited him. I should like to read what Mr. Baldwin said at the conclusion of the Ottawa conference:

Over that conference it was fitting that your own Prime Minister, the Prime Minister of Canada, should preside, and fortunate have we been that in Canada's Prime Minister we have a man so admirably qualified for that difficult task. He possesses a power of drive given to few, which is an essential element in the conduct of business of this kind. He has a grasp of detail which is astonishing, and yet with all, when one realizes what a grasp of detail involves, I have been struck all the time by his accessibility, that he has always been ready to discuss points as they arise with any delegation at any hour and in any place.
Empire Trade Agreements

Nothing could more completely contradict the case which the right hon. gentleman and his followers have endeavoured to build up since that conference, to the effect that the Prime Minister had taken a dictatorial attitude at that time. I venture to say that when the minor details of that conference have been forgotten, the memory that will be outstanding in the minds of those who attended will be the particular characteristics of the Prime Minister that made it a success, as stated so well by Right Hon. Stanley Baldwin.

The other day in his address the right hon. leader of the opposition stated that he sat in the gallery and listened to the opening remarks of Mr. Baldwin. I think it only fair to the people of the country, and especially to hon. members of this house, that I take this opportunity of putting on record, by way of contrast to the attitude of the right hon. gentleman now, a verbatim statement given by him and appearing in the Toronto Daily Star of September 28, 1932, in an interview with Mr. R. E. Knowles:

I observed you, Mr. King, at the conference's opening, sitting in the gallery, beside Sir Robert Borden. Did' you and he suffer much? I mean, did you exceedingly long to be in the game? Did you not feel you could have done it better yourself?""
Mr. King only stroked the dome of St. Paul's, afore referred to, and laughed. ""It was a great relief,"" he said-

In this you have the picture of a man who for nine years was prime minister of the country, clearly stating his great relief at being out of it all, with no urge, no thrill, no call of duty to see what contribution he could make. He was glad that it was possible for him to escape the effort.

The right hon. gentleman stated that Conservative members of parliament have been going around the country suggesting that if he is returned to power he will cancel the Ottawa agreements, and he has intimated that this is not correct. I should like to quote from one of the most partisan Liberal newspapers in western Canada, the Moose Jaw Times of October 19, 1933, which says:

We venture to predict that one of the first and major matters that Canada will expect of Mackenzie King and the Liberal party- when returned to power so soon as Premier Bennett provides a general election-will be a cancellation of the Bennett trade agreements-

This resolution has been placed before the house, Mr. Speaker, so that the people of Canada may know just where the right bon. gentleman stands in connection with this matter. He has stated that he has not
changed his attitude since the Ottawa agreements were signed in 1932, and I should like to put on record what his attitude was at that time. I quote from Hansard of October 17, 1932:

How can we be expected to support them, and still preserve our self-respect in the matter of supporting our own principles? ... I say the principle imbedded here is wholly indefensible and is undeserving of any support from any part of the British empire.

column1: To complete the record of the Liberal government with regard to Canada's trade with Great Britain, let me say that every concession that was given by Canada to Grpat Britain was the result of Liberal administration of affairs in this country. Take, for instance, the first 25 per cent preference in 1897; then the increase to 331 per cent some
Empire Trade Agreements

four or five years later. The next preference to be extended to Great Britain is in what was known as the Dunning budget. I want this house and' the country to realize the condition that was created in the mind of the British purchaser as a result of nine years of Liberal rule in this country under the leadership of the right hon. gentleman who now leads the opposition in this house. In one of the government publications published in the summer of 1930 there is this report of conditions obtaining in England with regard to Canadian produce. It is headed, ""Canada Week in Bristol, England,"" and reads:

May 1, 1930-""Canada Week"" designed as part of the publicity campaign that is bringing to the notice of British people the immense variety of Canada's products has just been successfully held in Bristol, England.

Five hundred leading stores gave up their windows to attractive displays of Canadian goods and tens of thousands of the public entered for a competition based on the varying popularity of what they saw or purchased.
Importers and wholesalers report a marked increase in demand and it may be said that Canada is definitely on the map so far as the west of England is concerned.

The lord mayor and city council gave the ""Canada Week"" the fullest civic support. Premises were taken in the heart of the city for the headquarters of the campaign to ""boost"" Canadian products and here thousands of samples were sold every day.
That was the condition of Canadian trade with Great Britain in 1930; but what happened in 1930?

In 1930 we had a promiser go up and down this country. Notwithstanding that Canada then was prosperous, so prosperous that to-day Conservative speakers will not compare their record with that year or the years before it, we had a promiser go up and down this country saying: What you want is high tariffs in Canada. And now, Mr. Speaker, I come to the subject of wheat. ""Listen, you agriculturists of western Canada and the rest of Canada""-I am going back to June 10, 1930. ""Listen, you agriculturists of western Canada and the rest of Canada, you who have been taught to mock at tariffs and applaud free trade; tell me when did free trade ever fight for you. I will make tariffs fight for you. I will use tariffs to blast a way into the markets of the world."" Those were the effervescent statements that won the election of 1930; and while my hon. friends opposite may gloat over the fact that numerically they have a majority in the house to put this motion
through, I challenge them to appeal to the acid test of public opinion in Canada and see what will be the result.

At the time those statements were made by the present Prime Minister, Canadian wheat was selling for SI. 10 a bushel, on June 10, 1930. What is the price to-day? hon. friends opposite used in our western country in the election campaign of 1930 showed a Canadian wheat farmer standing in the middle of a wheat field shouting to a diminutive picture of the then leader of the government, ""What are you going to do for my wheat?"" Well, if he had the same concern about doing something for the farmer with wheat at $1.10 a bushel, what is the situation now with wheat at half that price?

High tariffs were to be the panacea that was going to cure all the ills of the country. The first imperial conference took place and the Prime Minister went to Great Britain and told the people of that country that they must maintain an open market for us, that they must impose a duty of ten per cent against the rest of the world so that we might have a preference. He was turned down. The Minister of Agriculture quotes the final message of Mr. Stanley Baldwin to the present Prime Minister of Canada as Mr. Baldwin was leaving this country. Naturally, an Englishman is a gentleman, and in leaving the country Mr. Baldwin wanted to pay as nice a compliment as he could to the man whose guest he had been. Why did not the Minister of Agriculture quote what Mr. Thomas said? Why did he not quote what Snowden said? Snowden said, ""If you adopt the ten per cent tariff, then we are on the slippery slope that will lead to the bottomless pit."" And there was Mr. Thomas with his ""humbug.""

The first imperial conference proved a fiasco, and at the second imperial conference we were supposed to get a preference of six cents a bushel on our wheat. Is there anyone in this house who will raise his hand and say that as a result of that agreement he got one cent of an increase in the price of his wheat, let alone six cents a bushel? But we did get something else out of that agreement. We again got a dose of high tariff which put us further into the mire than we had been
Empire Trade Agreements

in before. We are told in the schedule attached to the agreement that Canada would give a preference to Great Britain in connection with a certain number of articles, and here again I want to pay tribute to the astuteness of the British bargainer. What do you suppose some of these articles were? What were some of the concessions which we gave to Great Britain in return for the supposed six cents a bushel on our wheat? To begin with, mickey mouse periodicals, No. 171 of the schedule. If any of my hon. friends opposite have any doubt about it let them refer to the article. Then we find automobiles from Great Britain, free of duty. There are two kinds of automobiles we could import from Great Britain, the millionaire's car and the little baby Austin, and I should like to see the baby Austin in operation on some of our sideroads in this country.

An evening or two ago, at the close of the session, I went down to get my mail and I got a government publication published under the auspices of the Minister of Public Works- a government report. I opened the book and in the dim and dismal light surrounding the post office I saw the almost nude picture of a man. I wondered whether it was Mussolini or Hitler or the rotund figure of my right hon. friend the Prime Minister. When I got to my room where there was a light I found that it was a picture of Job, the title being ""Job in his Misery."" Well, we are all familiar with the biblical story; we know what misery Job suffered, and we would be a hardhearted generation if we did not sympathize to the fullest extent with him in his affliction. But there are human boils and economic boils, and I do not need to tell the farmer and the labouring man of Canada that this country has had economic boils

during the last five years. And what are some of the boils it has had? Tariff ruination for one thing. I have here a statement in connection with western agriculture which I should like to put on record. These are authentic figures. The Minister of Agriculture put some figures on Hansard and they may be authentic too, but it would take a generation to read them over and compare them.

In the United States a Ford truck can be bought for 595 bushels of potatoes; in Canada it would take 3,200 bushels to buy the same truck. A turkey rancher in the United States can buy a Ford truck for 2,795 pounds, whereas it would take 6,600 pounds of turkey in Canada to buy the same truck here. In the United States a cattle man can exchange six steers for a Ford truck whereas his brother the Canadian farmer would have to sell thirty Canadian steers at the price in this country if he wanted the same truck here. And if wheat is sold in the United States to buy the truck, the United States grain grower can get the Ford truck f.o.b. Detroit for 468 bushels of wheat, whereas the Canadian wheat grower would have to give in exchange, for the same truck in Canada, 1,082 bushels of No. 1 northern Canadian wheat.

Mr. TURlNBULL: The right hon. leader of the opposition says they are ready to trade on a reciprocal basis; so are we. A few years ago he was not prepared to trade on a reciprocal basis; he was prepared to give Great Britain a fifty per cent preference, getting nothing in return. That is not a reciprocal basis. My hon. friends say it would be good for this country to give Great Britain a fifty per cent preference, on the old theory that you cannot sell unless you buy. If we should give it to Great Britain on that theory surely we should give it to the United States on the same basis; and if it would improve our sales in Great Britain surely a fifty per cent reduction would increase our sales in the United States, and in Germany, and in France, and all over the world. But my hon. friends do not urge that. They urged a fifty per cent reduction in 1919; the leader of the opposition then said that by that pledge he would stand or fall, but for nine years the only thing he did towards putting it into effect was to move in the opposite direction, finding it necessary to require that textiles should have a fifty per cent empire content instead of thirty-three and a third. The old content was restored by this government when they came back into office, and the British people appreciated' it.

Mr. Dunning realized the position; he knew we had only one market left for agricultural products, but he did not believe he could get a reciprocal treaty, because he said the British people would never tax foodstuffs. Believing he could not get a reciprocal treaty and a real preference he tried for the next best thing, a sentimental preference, and in order to do that he reduced the duty on a number of articles coming from Great Britain and increased the duty on similar articles coming from the United States and other countries.

The right hon. leader of the apposition objected because increases in the tariff were set out in these treaties. There were increases in the tariff under the Dunning budget, put through for the very same reason the tariff was increased under these treaties, to divert trade now going to the United States, who would not buy our goods, to Great Britain, who would buy our goods. Duties were increased under the Dunning budget just as they were under these treaties; they were fine in the Dunning budget, but they were anathema when put through by a Conservative government. The right hon. gentleman will remember that on one occasion he made a treaty with Australia, and in order to give Australia a preference on raisins he raised the duty on raisins coming into this country from the United States and other countries to three and a half cents per pound, 92582-38

For instance, we had no duty on ethylene glycol prior to these treaties, but in order to give Great Britain a preference we imposed a tariff of 15 per cent in the intermediate and general tariffs, leaving it free from Great Britain. That was what we did in connection with cream separators, to which my hon. friend from Yorkton referred. They were free across the board when we came into office. We imposed a duty of 25 per cent under the intermediate and general tariffs with free entry from Great Britain, and the country from which they come free is the country that fixes the price. The prices are lower to-day than they were when we came into office.

It was the Liberal policy of 1930 to give a sentimental preference in the hope that thereby they would reap some benefit. That was on the theory that you must buy in order to sell. When I was a boy I was taught that I must sell in order to get the money to buy. My Liberal friends, as usual, have things upside down and do the buying first. Let us examine this proposition of buying in order to sell. Suppose we had given Great Britain the complete Canadian textile market, had closed up all our own textile mills and prohibited the importation of textiles from any other country, so that Great Britain would have all the business. Then, having done that, suppose a British miller started out to buy a cargo of wheat for his mills, knowing he had to sell his flour in competition with the rest of the world. Suppose he was offered a cargo of Canadian wheat at $1 a bushel and a cargo of Argentine wheat of comparable quality at 99 cents a bushel. Which would he buy? We all know that he would buy the Argentine wheat, just as you or I would, and that is a complete answer to the argument that you must buy in order to sell. I think it is a complete answer to any onesided arrangement. As the right hon. leader of the opposition said in his younger days, when he was a little more obstreperous than he is now, if I may use the expression, trade cannot be a jug-handled proposition; it must work both ways. Now if my hon. friends opposite are in favour of freer trade they ought to vote for these treaties because they gave us freer trade. Our exports to all countries in 1933 amounted in round figures to $160,000,000; in 1934 they were $231,000,000, an increase of 44 per cent. Our exports to foreign countries increased from $85,000,000 to $117,000,000, an increase of 37 per cent, while our exports to the United States increased from $51,000,000 to $82,000,000, an increase of 61 per cent; and our imports increased accordingly. That shows that by our tarff agreements we have succeeded in getting freer trade with other countries, and having got it, and thereby increased the purchasing power in our own country, we were able then to buy and sell more goods in our own country.

But there are other benefits that arise from the treaties that have not yet been touched on so far as I know. The first is that by these treaties we escaped the British Import Duties Act. It did not need any act of the British government to make those duties effective. The act was passed in the spring of 1932 and automatically was to become effective in November of that year unless a treaty was made. If the treaty had not been made our goods going into Great Britain would have been subject to a duty of ten per cent or higher in all those lines of agricultural products that we have been selling to Great Britain since then. That alone is sufficient or should be sufficient to obtain the support of all members from all corners of the house.
Empire Trade Agreements

But in addition to that fact there was a clause in the treaty which prevented dumping on the British market. That clause is so important that I intend to read it in full. It is article 21 of the treaty, as follows:

This agreement is made on the express condition that if either government is satisfied that any preferences hereby granted in respect of any particular class of commodities are likely to he frustrated in whole or in part by reason of the creation or maintenance directly or indirectly of prices for such class of commodities through state action on the part of any foreign country, that government hereby declares that it will exercise the powers which it now has or will hereafter take to prohibit the entry from such foreign country directly or indirectly of such commodity into its country for such time as may be necessary to make effective and to maintain the preferences hereby granted by it.

This was the article that was invoked by the Canadian government to prevent the agreement being made by the British Timber Distributors Limited, the agreement that was under discussion in the house here to-day. Every member of this house knows what happened in 1932. Russia having ruined her ruble for foreign purposes by inflation, and desiring foreign exchange, was under the necessity of selling something to some other country in order to get foreign exchange to pay for her five year plan. The result was that she elected to take wheat as one of the articles that she would sell. She took it from her people to the point of starving millions of them to death and dumped it on the English market at whatever price she could get for it, driving the price of wheat down to the lowest level that it had reached in England for years. As a result we in western Canada were getting about 20 cents a bushel at the shipping point for first class varieties of wheat. That was the condition that prevailed in 1932. But article 21 of the agreement, which I have just read, prohibits that sort of thing, and if anything of that kind does happen all we have to do is appeal to the British government and have them put into effect article 21 with regard to the dumping of that product into Great Britain. The result has been an increased value for our wheat in the British market, and in that one item alone the treaty has been of immense value to the western farmer. We have had an increase in the price of our wheat from 43 cents to as high as SI a bushel. The price is a little depressed at the present moment by reason of a case with respect to gold that is now pending in the United States courts.
Under these treaties we increased not only our business with the United Kingdom but our business with the other countries of the empire. I have here the figures of our exports
