NEILL (Comox-Alberni):,,CANADA'S EXPORTS TO NEW ZEALAND,,,Mr. Speaker, for the first two weeks of this session every party in this house made a very sincere effort to abstain from partisan political strife, and in most cases the effort was successful. We made unprecedented progress with the business and the debates were kept upon a high plane. Then the hon. member for Toronto Scarborough (Mr. Harris) was prompted to bring in this motion and by so doing he pulled the plug out of the boat. The flag of truce came down with a run and the House of Commons was suddenly transformed from a legislative body into a political hustings. So it will continue to the end of this debate.

I feel strongly tempted to follow the example of the last speaker (Mr. Woods-worth), and say that I will vote against the motion just for that reason. The introduction at this time of this resolution was totally uncalled for. The agreements are not on the legislative program of this session; they are not up for revision or alteration in any sense. If the government wish to get a verdict on their actions in that regard, they will get a verdict from the people at the polls. The fact that this motion is passed by their usual large majority will not affect the issue one iota in the country, and we are wasting a great deal of time when we should be getting on with more important business. The hon. member who introduced the motion began mildly and in general terms, but he had not got into his stride very far before he turned it into a political appeal of a partisan character to the people at large. The introduction of the two flags at the close of his remarks gave just that nice touch of political patriotism without which some people seem to think no speech is complete when presented to the people of Canada.
The motion as introduced is a trick. It demands yes or no to a specific question which

is not capable of being intelligently answered yes or no. It is like the old gag of asking a candidate if he had stopped beating his wife, or of the curate who, embarrassed by discovering when he was the guest of his bishop that he was eating a bad egg, said that it was good in spots. This is a similar matter; these treaties are good in spots. It would be very remarkable if they were not. I presume they had some good effect in connection with apples and hogs. I take the word of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Weir) for that rather than my own knowledge, because these matters have not cut any issue in the district which I represent. I will take his word for it that they have been productive of good on those particular types of industry. Then as regards lumber they also have been of some benefit, helping us get an alternative market to that destroyed by other policies. I am willing to give credit for such benefits, although I regret to say that they did not produce much improvement in the district in which I live.

The hon. member who introduced this motion, and indeed every speaker on both sides, has played up statistics; they can prove anything by statistics, more so at the present time than ever before I think, because there was a distinct drop in prices and trade and then a distinct uplift. It is therefore easy, by taking either two succeeding years or months, or going back two or three years to produce any result whatsover from the same set of figures quite sincerely without any manipulation of them except in the way they are presented. I have here a string of instances by which I could prove that while no doubt the statement as to increased trade with the empire is correct, in many cases you find that, it was accompanied by still greater increases in our foreign trade. I am not going to press that because as I say with figures you can prove anything. I am going to quote only one instance. I shall take it, as I suppose other hon. members take their information, from the bulletins of the Dominion Bureau of Statistics. I call this to the attention of the present Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Hanson); I am sorry he is not in his seat. I do not accuse him of any wrongdoing;

I simply call his attention to it and suggest that he should instruct his deputies and clerks to be more careful. This stuff that is got out from day to day and from week to week is I think intended largely as propaganda on behalf of the government, and I do not object to that provided the figures are accurate. This is from the hulletin of Tuesday, January 22, 1935:
Empire Trade Agreements
Canada's Imports
December, 1934
December, 1933
Difference

This difference is said to represent eight per cent, and it is not a clerical error, because the word eight is written out. But if any hon. member will check that I think he will find it is not eight per cent but -8 or eight-tenths of one per cent. That is just one thing I picked up casually the other day. If they are all no more reliable than that, what is the use of quoting statistics? And while it says there has been this increase in empire trade of less than one per cent, in the case of foreign countries it was fourteen per cent.

I could give a lot of other instances such as increased imports from the British empire of one per cent and from foreign countries of thirteen per cent; or decreased imports from the United Kingdom of over one per cent while from the United States they increased twenty per cent. But as I say I am not going to press that; I am merely giving it to illustrate that you can prove anything from figures. The real fact is that these increased figures that everyone is quoting to his own advantage result from the general improvement in trade and not solely from the Ottawa agreements. If they were due solely to the Ottawa agreements then the increase in trade would be reflected in the trade with the British empire only, whereas I could give half a dozen instances in which it is shown to a far greater extent in trade with foreign countries.

I turn back to some notes of a speech I made on October 25, 1932, dealing with this subject-a rather rash speech; I was taking upon myself the role of a prophet and trying to foresee conditions as they would happen in years to come. However I am not greatly dissatisfied with the result; while perhaps I exaggerated in one respect there are other things I did not foresee that have turned out to be a disadvantage to the district I represent. I see I said:
We will all hope it turns out better than we believe it will-but always looking forward to a world conference.

I was emphasizing that what I hoped for was a satisfactory outcome of the world conference; that it failed was not the fault of this dominion or of the Prime Minister. I stated that on butter there was to be a preference of ten per cent but that it was largely nullified by the fact that the same privilege was given to New Zealand and to Australia; that these countries were our principal competitors and that it would be

practically impossible for us to meet the competition of New Zealand and to some extent that of Australia. I said I did not altogether blame the government for this, but that the preference given us was immaterial because our biggest competitor got it also. In regard to eggs I said that the preference was about eight to ten per cent, but unfortunately because of our distance we could compete only with storage eggs, and we have to compete with eggs from Denmark, situated close to the English markets, delivered fresh daily, and that owing to the fact that at that time they depreciated their currency to the same extent as Great Britain they had a preference of twenty-five per cent over us. That particular factor has now passed away. In connection with eggs I also referred to the much greater benefit it would have been if the government had given us relief in connection with freight rates on grain to British Columbia. I give the Prime Minister credit, for I believe it was entirely due to him, that since then we have got a small measure of redress for that grievance, but not to the extent we should, and only on a small part of the traffic.

Then we come to the question of fish and-lumber, and I see I said that Mr. Tolmie, the premier of the province, understood that fish and lumber were to get a twenty per cent preference, but when he heard that Great Britain refused to give more than ten per cent because Canada held back on textiles he-wired to Ottawa emphatically protesting against the two basic industries in the west being sacrificed on account of secondary industries in the east, and I gave him credit for so doing.

As to lumber, we did not get a preference on props or lumber for shipbuilding, and while we may or may not have got a preference on shingles-I forget if we did-it was of no use anyway because of course the British people do not use wooden shingles, on their houses. The ten per cent was not sufficient, although I frankly admit that the results were better than I expected.
column2: We

column1: received some little help from the fact that the exchange was favourable to us, but we have now lost that. What I think helped: us more than anything was the very unusual: situation that arose because Russia took it upon herself to arrest some British subjects and put them in gaol, and Britain stayed by her subjects and promptly put an embargo on all trade with Russia, a thing that would not happen again in a hundred years. That switched the trade to Canada, and British trade once directed into any course has a way-
Empire Trade Agreements

of staying put. Of course they had some lingering antipathy to the Russians for the way they had acted, which was very largely the cause of our getting a foothold in the lumber market of Great Britain. But it is uphill work; it is a long haul. There is a handicap against us of about $10 per thousand feet on the haul. Then there is the fall clause always hanging over our heads, and section 21 has been discovered not to be as effective as we supposed. A great basic fact is that Russia is an enormous buyer of goods from Great Britain, and Britain is first and last a salesman; she wants to sell, and Russia cannot pay gold for everything she buys, therefore she has to sell goods; that is a large factor at the back of the desire you see in Britain to buy lumber from Russia.
The trade we lost to the United States-I am not going to give figures; they have been given in the house before-was not compensated by the trade we got from Britain.

Then as to the fish business, I see I said that the canners wanted a specific duty because that would help them best in competition against Japan, which had an enormous advantage over us because their yen was badly depreciated. But the canners did not get a specific duty. They then asked for twenty per cent; they got ten per cent, which was not enough. And here are the results:

In spite of the Ottawa preference Canada sold Great Britain only about one-third as much canned salmon in February. 1933, as in February, 1932. Both Russia and the United States increased their sales greatly. There must be a reason.

Then in the bulletin of the Department of Trade and Commerce, which I assume to be correct in this ease, I find that in 1933 Canada was third in the imports of canned salmon into Great Britain, with 45,833 hundredweights. The United States was first with something over 161,000 hundredweights and soviet Russia was second with over 91,000 hundredweights. Two years ago Canada was first with over 80,000 hundredweights, but under these so called preferential advantages we have dropped to 45,000 hundredweights.

Now I come to a situation which particularly concerns the people whom I represent; I refer to coal. I can hardly be expected to hold up both hands in wild enthusiasm for the treaties when the coal miners whom I represent have been badly hit in connection with the import of coal. It is now possible, and in fact it has been encouraged under the treaties, to import coal from Great Britain, the mining of which has been subsidized by

the British government. We cannot put on any duty or any dumping duty because of these treaties. It is brought out practically as ballast in ships coming to Vancouver to load wheat; part of it comes in free and part at a reduced rate of duty, but because of the provisions of the treaty we cannot put on a dumping duty. Another grievance in this regard is that the tariff board, which is a faint but expensive echo of a few autocratic gentlemen in the customs department, has ruled that the production of 900 tons of coal does not constitute production in Canada. Therefore they have ruled that we could not put a dumping duty on that coal brought here from Great Britain in that way. But when it suited them to do so they put a high duty on tin for the benefit of some manufacturer in eastern Canada. Our cannery men in the west cannot buy their tin from that plant because of the long rail haul; they have to get their tin either from the United States or from Great Britain by water, and consequently they have to pay the duty. An opportunity arose for some relief in that regard because a certain class of tin was not being manufactured in 'Canada, but the manufacturers were on the alert. They started what I was going to call a two by four factory, but it was not that big; it was a little one horse concern that could have been put in a chicken house. They turned out a few cases of these tins and that was considered to constitute production in Canada. But the production of 900 tons of coal did not constitute the production of coal in Canada. So the cannery men should not be expected to support the operation of these treaties.

Then I come to the question of wheat. I am not going into that matter in detail; men better qualified than I have dealt with it, but I must say that we appear to have made one grand mess of the wheat situation if this statement is true :

The spread between Canadian and Argentine wheat prices has not only kept Canadian wheat and flour out of importing countries but it has been so wide that British millers import the Argentine product, mill it in Britain and in the first nine months of this year have shipped 50,425 barrels of it back to Canada for domestic consumption.

Is that not a remarkable thing, that Argentine flour milled in Britain should be imported into Canada? Possibly it is being used on our prairies, when we cannot sell our own wheat. This article also states that we imported 60,000 barrels of Australian soft wheat flour brought in via the old country. In the meantime we are losing the European market
Empire Trade Agreements
I have another objection to these treaties.

I understood that we were going to ease up on our restrictions on British goods, but we are not easing up at all. Time and again I have had retailers complain to me of the conditions undeT which they import goods from Great Britain. They have shown me the invoices and the customs memorandums. They never know, when they buy something from Great Britain, what the ultimate cost will be; weeks and sometimes months after the goods are sold and paid for the customs people come along and rake up some new change or ruling and the retail men have to pay up. They have no remedy. Trade will never increase under conditions like those; the British people and the Canadian buyers get disgusted.

If I might digress for a moment I should say that we have too many rulings and regulations in Canada. We are not governing here in this house; the country is governed by the men in the government offices, the customs offices and these other places, who make the rules and regulations. We are being governed by an autocratic body of officials who are not responsible to God or man. That is what we are suffering from. Someone once said ""Allow me to write the poems of a nation and I care not who makes its laws."" I could say, ""Let me make the rules and regulations and I care not who makes the laws,"" because to suit myself I can make rules and regulations that are not justified in carrying out the purpose of the act, and that are practically acts by themselves.
The hon. member who introduced this resolution said, at page 356 of Hansard:

. . . and in another fifty years' time history will tell that the standard of living of the people in the Ukraine, Roumania. Bulgaria, will be raised by the consumption of the manufactured goods from the industrial part of Europe.""

That was what someone had told him, and from that he drew the inference that these pacts would be all right. Well, fifty years is a long time hence, and I wonder if the hon. member knows that in regard to many of the articles included such as cheese, butter, milk products, poultry and so on, the treaties expire this year, and that with regard to the other commodities they expire in two years. So there is not much for the Balkans to acquire a new standard of living. Already we have got down to quotas. The British Minister of Agriculture, Mr. Elliott, has gone in for protection and, like the British people, he is doing it thoroughly.

He is going to make Great Britain self sustaining agriculturally as far as possible, and he has a very good weapon to his hand. There is an enormous bonus on wheat, for example, and when he has managed to encourage the production of wheat or beef or butter, as the case may be, to the point where there is danger of a poor market, he can provide a good market by a wave of the hand. He can simply say to Canada and New Zealand, ""Ship in less; put on a quota"" and that will provide his market, but we will have to pay the price. The boast has been made that the Prime Minister induced Great Britain to go in for protection. If that is so I think he has a good deal to answer for, because I think it has been the curse of the Canadian agricultural producer; we are losing the best market we ever had or ever will have.

Let me give you a homely illustration of how quotas work. Last year, in the height of the depression, when I went home I told a good friend of mine that I was going to buy, and I did buy, thirty ricks of firewood from him; but I did not buy all I wanted from him; I bought ten or fifteen ricks from somebody else. It would be a suitable comparison if I went to my friend this year and said, "" I am going to make a treaty with you which will be very much to your advantage. I am going to give you all my business in firewood this year; I am not going to buy from anybody else, but I am going to buy a good deal of coal and I am only going to need eight ricks of wood."" Would he prefer to sell me thirty ricks in an open market, in open competition, or would he be gratified to be told that he was going to have a complete monopoly of my trade, but could sell only eight ricks? I think that is a fair illustration, even though it is a humble one.

I am not deprecating trade treaties with Great Britain. I was bom there; my forebears lie there, and I am not likely to take the attitude that we should not Have trade treaties with Great Britain. But I should like to do business in Mr. Baldwin's way. He sat not many feet from where I am standing now and urged that the measure of preference given to Great Britain should not be obtained by raising high tariffs against other nations but should be secured by reducing tariffs against British imports. That is what must be done if we are to get on a satisfactory basis. We want treaties not only with Great Britain but with the whole world, but as a result of these treaties we are unable to make agreements with other countries because the tariff
Empire Trade Agreements

in the intermediate column is so high they do not want to do business with us, and we cannot give them the British preference because that is confined to Great Britain alone. Consequently we have nothing to offer, and these agreements stand in the way. I believe I speak for the province of British Columbia when I say that we want to sell our fish, lumber, copper and our coal and we want to sell it in the best market, namely the nearest market. At the same time we want to be free to deal with the whole world in exactly the same way and in the same spirit as that in which Great Britain has dealt with the world. Great Britain always has wanted and I believe always will want to deal with the whole world. That is the policy that has made Britain great, and has made the British empire the greatest in history. That policy has made Britain great and prosperous, and I believe if we follow her example we too will become great and prosperous.

Yes, as 1929 proved, unless we act, and act now. How can we hope to secure and hold the British market? There is only one answer, only one way, and that is by buying goods from Britain who in turn will buy our wheat.

Mr. Dunning said that there was only one way, and that was to get a treaty with Great Britain as quickly as possible, and that our only hope was the British market. This government got that British market. 1048669,ca.proc.d.1935-02-07.9.95,1935-02-07,6be06326-5c16-4c0b-9f3e-0764dae4556b,ca.m.3509,Mr. LOUCKS:,,CANADA'S EXPORTS TO NEW ZEALAND,,,Yes. I do not pretend to be a debater, Mr. Speaker. I am just an ordinary farmer, but I throw out a challenge to the hon. member for Yorkton, lawyer as he is, to come up to Biggar in my constituency of Rosetown and I will debate the treaties with him on any platform-a dirt farmer against a lawyer. I will go further and say that I will entertain the hon. gentleman if he will come. I would like to coax him to come up there, and I would like to see how far he will get in debating the treaties with just an ordinary farmer in the rural constituency of Rosetown.

I am sorry the hon. member for Humboldt (Mr. Totzke) is not in his seat. He was not successful in winning his nomination. Last spring he spoke on the marketing bill in this house, and apparently he sent the Hansard report of his speech to one of his supporters, a farmer, from whom I received a letter in which he says: ""I want to compliment you, Mr. Loucks, on your speech. Watch and see what will happen our member from Humboldt in the next election."" Well, Mr. Speaker, he did not have to wait till the next election because the hon. member did not even get his nomination. The hon. member for Humboldt replied to me that my career would be very short as a member of parliament, but I would like to say to him that he never got to first base; he could not get the nomination. What was the reason? I am told that the Liberals in Humboldt constituency have said: Because our member has opposed the treaties and the marketing bill we cannot elect him in this constituency. That is the reason why I believe he did not get the nomination. What about the hon. member for South Battleford (Mr. Vallance)? Was he successful in getting his nomination? No, he was defeated; he could not get the nomination.
I have it on very good authority that the Liberals in Kindersley were saying the same

thing, that the fact that their member had opposed the marketing bill and the treaties meant that Liberals in the constituency would not support him. I think I am right in what I am saying. I got it from reliable Liberals from that part of the country.

What happened in my own constituency at the nomination meeting on the tenth of August? Why bless you, Mr. Speaker, to my surprise we had over three hundred delegates who had taken time off from harvesting to attend that meeting, and the gentleman who got up and nominated me made it clear that he had never been a Conservative. He said he liked the very attitude of Mr. Loucks when he was speaking, and he complimented me on the stand that I had taken, and said that it gave him great pleasure to get up and nominate me. He said some very flattering things about this government and myself in nominating me. It was a surprise to me because he is not a Conservative at all. This same gentleman, a lawyer in Outlook, informed me quite recently that when my campaign starts and we go on the hustings, ""I am at your service, Mr. Loucks.""

I wished to hold a meeting in my constituency some time before coming here for the session, and I went to see the school trustees to get .permission to use the school-house. My hon. friend from South Battle-ford must pass it every time he goes to Saskatoon. Here is what happened. I went to one of the trustees, knowing him to be a staunch Liberal, and asked him if I could have the schoolhouse. He said, ""Certainly, with pleasure, so far as I am concerned. I have been a Liberal; in the last provincial election I thought I had intelligence when I voted for the Liberals, but I got gypped."" He said that Mr. Gardiner and his bunch came out and said they would cancel the $10,000,000 in notes given to the federal government by western farmers, a matter which the provincial government had nothing to do with, and he said, ""I have had all I want to do with the Liberal party."" When I got to the meeting after advertising it, as I always do, T asked the audience to appoint a chairman, and they told me to appoint my own chairman. I said, ""I will call on Mr. Weir."" Mr. Weir was one of the school trustees, and they weTe surprised when I called on him to act as chairman because he was a staunch Liberal. But Mr. Weir came forward and said it was a pleasure to act as chairman for me on that occasion, 'because I had had the courage to speak in the house in defence of the marketing bill and the empire trade treaties. I wonder how many Liberals in

Saskatchewan are feeling the same way. They have not such short memories. They have not forgotten what has been taking place here in Ottawa, and they know that the Prime Minister has carried out what was the policy of Mr. Dunning, and has put it into actual practice. Mr. Dunning meant every word of that policy, and I have every respect for him. I think it is up to the members of this house who come from the west to speak in support of these treaties. The farmers all over this country know that if it had not been for the British market which we got as a result of these treaties, we would have had no market for our agricultural products, and the hon. member for Regina (Mr. Turnbull) has quoted facts and figures to prove my statement and the truth of Mr. Dunning's statement.

Sometimes I wonder whether hon. gentlemen opposite are sincere when they say they want to have this question decided by a vote. So far as I am concerned I hope they will get the opportunity because it will do me an awful lot of good in the Rosetown constituency. I am sorry the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Brown) is not in his seat at the moment. If my memory serves me aright it was in 1932 that the hon. member, for whom I have a great respect, got up and said that he had about fifty hogs, and he said, ""I wish I had knocked them on the head."" That was when they were worth 2j cents a pound. I think he must be glad he did not knock them on the head now that hogs are to 9 cents a pound. Yet the hon. gentleman gets up and tries to discredit the treaties, notwithstanding that they have increased the price to him on the bacon type by nearly 6 cents a pound.

Let me assure my hon. friends to your left, Mr. Speaker, that so far as I am concerned, and I think I speak for those representing this government from Saskatchewan, the people resent the attitude of the party opposite towards these treaties and the other measures that have been brought down. I wonder when I hear the leader of the opposition expressing his anxiety to get down to business why hon. members behind him should get up and discredit all that the Prime Minister indicated in his broadcast, because that is not the attitude of the leader of the opposition himself. He would like to see these measures placed on the statute books as quickly as possible; but if they have no more merit than some of his followers can see in them, then I fail to see why he should want to have them embodied in legislation.

If I had time, there are many things which I should like to say in regard to the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act and its operation in Saskatchewan, but I will not weary the house at the moment with a discussion of that subject. I must confine my remarks to the resolution. I want to assure members on the other side that I have fairly good reason to know the attitude of the farmers of the west, and particularly of Saskatchewan, and I think I can safely say to-night, from what has happened in the last few months, that we shall send down from our province at the next election fifteen members on this side out of the twenty-one.

1048672,ca.proc.d.1935-02-07.9.98,1935-02-07,1d6a8f18-7d15-4909-b0f5-88f9b514f20a,ca.m.1201,Miss AGNES MACPHAIL (Southeast Grey):,,CANADA'S EXPORTS TO NEW ZEALAND,,,I wish to associate myself with the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) in his attitude toward this resolution. I do feel that it is a very dangerous precedent for us to set. Are we going to go over legislation which is two or three years old? If so we are certainly laying out a good deal of extra work for ourselves in the future. It is a most extraordinary procedure for us to be asked now to approve of the operation of the treaties. The resolution asks us to say whether or not the operation of the trade agreements has been beneficial to Canada. I doubt very much whether anyone can answer that question. I think it is much too soon for us to know. There are a great
Empire Trade Agreements

many factors which we cannot weigh for a considerable time yet. If the temporary gains that have been made in hog prices-and I am inclined to think that the agreements had some effect on these prices-have been at such great cost as to lead to dissatisfaction and offence almost in Great Britain, as one is led to believe from many newspapers as well as from conversations with different people, all of which would show that there is a feeling in Great Britain not only against the treaties but against Canada because of them, then it seems to me that we are paying very dearly indeed for any temporary gains. Moreover, if by the treaties we have added to the cost of those things which we purchase from Great Britain, we have possibly more than eaten up all the benefits that would accrue. If the Canadian consumer and the British manufacturer are paying dearly for the advantage given the Canadian manufacturer, then I for one cannot say that the trade pacts have worked out beneficially to this country. I think it is quite possible, and time will likely prove it to be true, that the preferential arrangement within the empire has given offence to the world at large; the reaction of other countries to the preference within the empire will result in diverting their trade to those countries that are not involved in the agreements under discussion.

To me it is amusing-it is interesting to have something amusing in this house-to hear members of the government take so much credit for the rise in farm prices. Well, there is this you can say about farm prices now as compared with the 1932 level; they could scarcely have fallen further, because had they done so they would have fallen out of sight. If they were going to move they had to rise. If the government had been as much interested in farm prices in 1932 as they now appear to be, they would have depreciated Canadian currency and made it possible for Canada to take advantage to such extent as it could of the agreements at the time they were made. We were not able to avail ourselves of the agreements until the country to the south of us had taken such action in connection with monetary matters as brought the Canadian dollar to a parity with the pound. In other words, the government of Canada waited until another country had made it possible for this dominion to take whatever advantage it could of the British market. While the hon. member for Rosetown (Mr. Loucks) was shedding tears over the price the farmers got for hogs in 1932, he ought to have been willing to assume some responsibility in the matter, because the adverse exchange from which we
suffered then had a good deal to do with the prices we were receiving at that time for our hogs.

As I listened to the torrent of figures which flowed from the mouth of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Weir) before dinner, I was reminded of the broadcast of Colling and Colling over CFRB at 6.30, which I endure in order to hear Jim Hunter, who does much to justify the Telegram. As I listened to the figures which poured with such power from the minister's lips I could make nothing of them at all and I am sure that everybody in the house felt the same way. Possibly when one reads them in Hansard they may have meaning, but they certainly conveyed nothing to me as I heard them read. As I listened to the blasts of oratory from the hon. member for Yorkton (Mr. McPhee) I thought how very happy a position those hon. gentlemen are in; whatever their party does is right and whatever their leader does is just the thing to do. I wish I had the kind of mind that could put myself in that position. It is so happy.

There is no real assurance that the market which Canadian farm products now find in Great Britain will continue. It is well known to hon. members that the Minister for Agriculture in Great Britain, Mr. Elliott, .is pursuing a policy of self sufficiency in agricultural products within that country. Whether or not he can ever achieve this is another matter, but he at any rate is trying to do so and the very moment they are able to produce within their own country those things which they require, we shall see a very rapid dropping of exports from this country to Great Britain. Therefore I feel we are building on a false premise if we believe we are going to continue to ship to either Great Britain, or, indeed to other European countries -any great quantities of foodstuffs.

I believe some of the pools in Canada have approved the treaties, but if I can judge the pools from the cooperative company with which I have had something to do in Ontario, then it can be said that each pool considers the commodity which it handles, and if conditions or prices have been improved for that commodity, the pool then draws the conclusion, which is not always the correct one, that conditions have been improved for the people generally. But when we are considering a standard of living for the Canadian people-and I am thinking again of agriculture-two factors enter in, selling prices and living costs. It is true that selling prices are a great factor, but living costs are also,
Empire Trade Agreements
so if by the trade treaties we get increased living costs, that may more than counteract any increase in prices caused by them.

In closing I want to say only one other thing and that is, in my opinion it is dubious if world trade will again reach the volume of 1929. There are possibly a number of reasons for that, but certainly one of them is that to-day every country in the world is striving for self sufficiency and the success that has been attained by European countries in growing foodstuffs shows to what a degree this ideal, if it be an ideal, can be reached. If countries are going to become more and more self sufficient, then it is unlikely for a long time at any rate that the volume of trade will be again as great as in 1929.

There is another reason why trade is not increasing and that is lack of the medium of exchange. In this country we try to sell to other countries those goods which our own people would like to buy but cannot afford, and other countries are trying to sell to us their surplus goods which their own people, if they had a higher standard of living, could use but which they again have not the money to purchase. Therefore I think the root causes of a fall in the volume of trade are these two factors: On the one hand lack of sufficient money to effect an exchange of goods, and second, a growing sufficiency of all nations due in part to invention and energy and due in part to very many years of high tariffs by almost all countries in the world.

I certainly am not going to put myself in the ridiculous position of supporting a motion which is going to make us do the work of two years over again. We started this session in the rarefied atmosphere of high endeavour for a couple of weeks. To-day we fell back very far toward the bad old days. I hope we shall not stay in this particular state of mind too long, because I feel the temper of the Canadian people will not stand too much of the sort of exhibition that we have Rad to-day. I am going to vote against the -motion because I think it is one that should *not have been moved. It is one with which the house has nothing to do at this moment, and even if I agreed with it I would still vote against it, offered as it is at this time.

column1: If I want an opinion concerning the virtues of the Liberal party I would not go to the leader of the opposition, because I know what he would tell me. Nor would I go to the Prime Minister if I wanted to have the virtues of the Conservative party extolled; nor would I go to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre to learn of the merits of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation. I would go to more disinterested authorities. On the day this resolution was introduced I received a book entitled The Story of Canada's Industrial Expansion. On the front page I see the statement:
A remarkable record.

Not only has there been notable progress during the past ten years, but even through recent years of depression this progress has continued in a remarkable way, giving good ground for encouragement and providing a cheerful outlook for the current year.
Head the evidence in these articles on:
New industries established in Canada in the past four years;
And so on. This is reprinted from Industrial Canada of January, 1935, and published by the Canadian Manufacturers' Association.

who is interested only in the expansion of trade, Mr. Saunders, secretary of the Halifax board of trade, not a biased politician.

Those who consider that Nova Scotia is backward industrially, has few, if any, new industries, and is not expanding its manufacturing' operations, should read this impressive record-compiled by Mr. Saunders. It should be an, eye opener, for it reveals the establishment of quite a number of new factories within the-last few years and shows that the province by the Atlantic is making industrial progress, even in recent difficult times, as well as the rest of Canada.

I was interested in that. I take it that each of these articles would be from the pen of someone as disinterested politically as Mr. Saunders.
